title: Sadhu
hook: one word, three times, after a gift: what is the whole room agreeing to?
tomorrow: what were the Buddha's last words, and why those?

segments.voice: Yesterday, thus have I heard: evam me sutam, the source line that opens the discourses. Heard, not invented. Today, the word that often comes at the other end, when a teaching is over.
screen: `EVAM ME SUTAM.` → `THE WORD AT THE OTHER END.`

segments.voice: Crowds have their chants: a name shouted three times, a clap that builds. In a Lao or Thai temple, after the monks finish a blessing, or after a family hands over a gift of food or robes, the whole room answers with one word, three times: sadhu, sadhu, sadhu. Two odd things here. Why three times? And why does the same word, in India, name a wandering holy man with ash on his skin? Same word, a temple hall and a roadside. What's everyone agreeing to?
screen: `A CROWD'S CHANT.` → `SADHU, SADHU, SADHU.` → `WHY THREE? WHY A HOLY MAN?`

segments.voice: Start with the meaning. Sadhu: good. Well done. It is good. In the discourses, the Buddha sometimes says it himself to a disciple who has answered well: sadhu, sadhu, good, good. In Sanskrit and Hindi the same word also names a holy wanderer, and you can hear why: a sadhu is a good one, someone who has given things up. Same root of meaning, two lives. That's the first puzzle solved. Now, what is the room agreeing to? When a family gives a meal to the monks and the room says sadhu, the people saying it didn't cook. They're rejoicing in someone else's good. The tradition has a word for that, anumodana, and it rests on one of the twenty words from a few days ago: mudita, gladness at another's good. Saying sadhu turns somebody else's generosity into a joy the whole room can share, and teachers say rejoicing like that is itself a good act. Now the three. Here the old texts are quiet; they don't explain it. What's clear is the rhythm: the homage is chanted three times, the refuges a second time and a third. Sadhu falls into the same step. Good, good, good. Once to hear it, twice to mean it, three times to share it, as some put it.
screen: `SADHU: GOOD, WELL DONE.` · `A HOLY MAN: A GOOD ONE.` · `ANUMODANA: GLAD AT ANOTHER'S GOOD.` · `THREE: THE RHYTHM OF THE CHANTS.` · then, large: `SADHU, SADHU, SADHU.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind three good things other people did this week, small ones: a held door, a kind text, a meal someone made. For each, say sadhu once, quietly. Then sit, and let yourself be glad they happened, even though none of them was yours.
Sadhu: good, well done. Said three times after a teaching or a gift, to share in someone else's good.
Keep this one: sadhu, sadhu, sadhu, for somebody else's good, and a share of the joy. Twenty-five days of Pali.

howItsDone: In Theravada temples, people say sadhu three times, often with palms joined, after a Dhamma talk, a blessing, or an offering to the monks; some also say it on hearing of a good deed.

fork.setup: your cousin, the one you've always been compared to, gets into her dream school. you didn't apply anywhere yet. what does sadhu point to?
options: say congrats, and mean it: her good is yours to rejoice in.
hold off until you have good news of your own.
congratulate her, but mention it was mostly luck.
fork.reveal: sadhu is anumodana, rejoicing in someone else's good. the joy is open to anyone who says it, whoever did the deed.

original.note: Pali, in Devanagari letters: sadhu, good, well done; the same letters spell the Sanskrit word.

trapdoor: what you thought: a polite 'amen' at the end of a chant.
what it means: good, well done, said three times to rejoice in a teaching, a blessing or someone else's gift.
what a scholar hears: anumodana, joy in another's merit, treated by teachers as a good act of its own; and the same word, in Sanskrit, names a holy one.

peace, said as a greeting when entering a temple
goodbye, said by monks at the end of an alms round

chat.meaning: Sadhu means good, well done. Said after a teaching or a gift, it rejoices in someone else's good, three times over.

sadhu.meaning: good, well done; it is good

anumodana.meaning: rejoicing in someone else's good deed

sources.ref: sadhu: 'good, virtuous; well, very well' (also an exclamation of approval)

sources.ref: The Buddha's 'sadhu, sadhu' to disciples who answer well, e.g. MN 38 (Mahatanhasankhaya Sutta)

notes: Meaning of sadhu follows the PTS dictionary. 'In Sanskrit and Hindi the same word also names a holy wanderer… a good one' is a meaning link, not an etymology claim; confirm the Keeper is comfortable with 'same root of meaning'.
The Buddha saying 'sadhu, sadhu' to disciples: cited to MN 38 as an example; confirm the reference (it appears in many suttas; swap in a surer one if needed).
'Teachers say rejoicing like that is itself a good act' (anumodana as a ground of merit, pattanumodana among the ten punnakiriyavatthu in the commentaries) is hedged as teachers' view; confirm.

'Here the old texts are quiet' about the threefold sadhu: as far as known, no canonical text explains it; the rhythm link to the triple homage and refuges is offered as observation, and 'once to hear it, twice to mean it, three times to share it' is labeled 'as some put it'. Keeper may prefer to cut that line.
Hook: 'a wandering holy man with ash on his skin' describes some Hindu sadhus; no claim about all. Hindu reader may check the image is respectful.
